title: Scalable Differentially Private Data Compression via Diffusion and Stochastic Codes

paper.title: Scalable Differentially Private Data Compression via Diffusion and Stochastic Codes
paper.abstract:
Abstract The ever-increasing collection of personal data has created mounting pressure to develop technologies that protect sensitive aspects of individual identity.
Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled framework with strong formal guarantees and has already achieved practical success.
However, releasing high-dimensional data, such as images, has remained elusive: releasing uncompressed privatized data requires significant storage.
At the same time, no effective data compression scheme exists that can compress high-resolution data with privacy guarantees. We address this challenge with DP-DiPP , a compression pipeline that combines stochastic codes with diffusion models.
DP-DiPP is highly flexible: the practitioner has direct control over the compression rate-privacy-utility tradeoff.
As the theoretical backbone, we extend the Poisson private representation (PPR) of ( Liu et al., 2024 ) to encode the outputs of privacy mechanisms.
We then combine it with DiffC, a diffusion-based lossy data compression method, to obtain a differentially private image compressor.
Our experiments on privatized image classification on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that DP-DiPP significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving a 10-30 times better compression while retaining comparable privacy guarantees and utility.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Over the past decades, the rapid growth in data collection and its use in downstream systems such as machine learning has produced undeniable benefits. Yet, this has also raised serious concerns about the identifiability of sensitive information and individual privacy. Therefore, developing frameworks and algorithms that protect privacy is essential to ensure user trust. In this paper, we adopt differential privacy (DP) as the privacy framework, a stronger variant of DP ( Dwork et al., 2006 ; Dwork & Roth, 2014 , DP;) . DP has already found practical success, such as for collecting user data ( Erlingsson et al., 2014 ) , for releasing privatized tabular data, like census data ( United States Census Bureau, 2021 ) , and for preventing generative models from memorizing and revealing their training sets ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . Local DP (LDP) protects individuals’ data by requiring that a system’s output reveal only limited information about its input. In practice, this idea translates to randomizing the sensitive data X X before revealing it to an untrusted party, according to a privacy mechanism . For example, if X X represents location data, such as GPS coordinates ( Andrés et al., 2013 ) , one possible privacy mechanism is to add appropriately calibrated noise η \eta to the coordinates to prevent precise localization, that is, Y = X + η Y=X+\eta . Of course, we still wish to use the privatized data for some purpose. Hence, a natural tradeoff arises between the privatized data’s utility for its downstream task and its privacy guarantee. However, despite its success for tabular data, scaling DP to high-dimensional data such as images, audio, or video remains challenging. This difficulty stems from several factors. First, directly releasing privatized high-dimensional data can incur substantial storage and communication costs. Second, the noise required to provide meaningful privacy guarantees can severely degrade the data’s utility in high-dimensional domains. To the best of our knowledge, prior work has not systematically studied high-resolution privatized data compression, where the goal is to jointly preserve privacy, reduce storage cost, and retain downstream utility. This is the challenge we tackle in this paper. The theoretical foundation of our work is in the emerging field of data compression with stochastic codes ( Flamich, 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Flamich & Gündüz, 2026 ) . In practice, stochastic codes serve as a randomized lossy compression mechanism : for example, consider an input X X (modeled as a random variable) and a perturbed, lossy version Y = X + η Y=X+\eta , where η \eta is independent of X X . Then, for a given X X , stochastic codes produce a bitstring S S that encodes one sample of Y | X Y\mid X , such that the expected length of S S is as small as possible. By utilizing stochastic codes, the generated sample exactly follows the conditional distribution. This is in sharp contrast to traditional lossy compression, where we first construct a quantizer and then attempt to determine the quantizer’s error distribution. This flexibility of stochastic codes naturally suggests their application to compressing the output of privacy mechanisms, where the exactness of sample distribution preserves other desirable statistical properties of the original privacy mechanism, such as unbiasedness and Gaussianity. Unfortunately, as we explain in Section 2.2 , simply encoding the outputs of privacy mechanisms with stochastic codes can lose the privacy guarantees of the original mechanism; hence, we need to design special-purpose codes that preserve the guarantees. As a solution, we use the Poisson private representation ( Liu et al., 2024 , PPR;) as a starting point for our work, a stochastic code that does have LDP guarantees. Concretely, we develop an approximate version (called “step-limited” in this paper) of PPR that encodes any pure ϵ \epsilon -LDP mechanism, ensuring that its output is at least 2 ​ α ​ ϵ 2\alpha\epsilon -LDP, where α > 1 \alpha>1 is a tunable parameter that interpolates between the code’s privacy and the expected codelength. Unfortunately, applying PPR to complex data is challenging due to its generally very slow runtime, scaling super-exponentially with the information content. To circumvent this issue, we combine our extended PPR code with DiffC, a variable-rate, diffusion-based data compression framework ( Theis et al., 2022 ) . DiffC progressively encodes each denoising step of a Gaussian diffusion model, thereby decomposing the compression problem into smaller, manageable steps. However, additive Gaussian noise never yields a pure ϵ \epsilon -LDP mechanism. Hence, we approximate the Gaussian denoising targets at each step with moment-matched Laplace distributions, which do provide pure ϵ \epsilon -LDP guarantees, allowing us to apply our approximate PPR code. Somewhat surprisingly, we empirically find that this approximation does not degrade the denoiser’s performance, while significantly strengthening its formal privacy guarantee. Thus, we call our method Differentially Private DiffC with Poisson Processes (DP-DiPP, pronounced dippy-dip ). Put succinctly, DP-DiPP jointly compresses and privatizes the data, rather than privatizing the data first and then compressing it losslessly. Thus, to validate our method, we conduct experiments on privatized image compression and classification on CIFAR-10 and compare it with the naive method. We find that DP-DiPP performs significantly better, consistently reducing bitrate by a factor of 10-30 while maintaining a comparable pure LDP guarantee and utility (as measured by classification accuracy). In summary, our main contributions are as follows: • In Section 3 , we extend the Poisson private representation (PPR) of Liu et al. (2024) to approximate sampling, and analyze its output sample quality and its DP guarantees. Notably, we show that it yields a 2 ​ α ​ ϵ 2\alpha\epsilon -LDP certificate when used to encode any pure ϵ \epsilon -LDP mechanism, where α ≥ 1 \alpha\geq 1 is a tunable parameter that trades off privacy and approximation quality. • In Section 4 , we modify DiffC, a variable-rate, Gaussian diffusion-based lossy data compression method, by replacing the Gaussian targets in the denoising process with Laplace distributions, which turns the reverse process into a pure ϵ \epsilon -LDP mechanism. Surprisingly, we show that this approximation does not significantly degrade the denoiser’s performance. • In Section 5 , we apply our approximate PPR code to the modified DiffC process, yielding our proposed method, DP-DiPP , and validate its performance on a privatized image compression task on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Our results show that DP-DiPP consistently reduces bitrate by a factor of 10-30 while maintaining a comparable pure LDP guarantee and utility (as measured by classification accuracy).

sections.heading: 2.1 Privacy Mechanisms and Differential Privacy
sections.text: Differential privacy (DP) provides formal certificates that quantify how much information a system reveals about its input ( Dwork et al., 2006 ; Dwork & Roth, 2014 ) . In this paper, we concern ourselves with its strict variant, local DP (LDP): we take some sensitive input x x and randomize it using a privacy mechanism M ⁡ ( x ) M(x) to reduce the information leaked by x x . However, not any randomization will do: in ε \varepsilon -LDP we choose a privacy parameter ε ≥ 0 \varepsilon\geq 0 and require the mechanism M M to satisfy, for any two inputs x , x ′ x,x^{\prime} and any measurable event S S , ℙ [ M ( x ) ∈ S ] ≤ e ε ℙ [ M ( x ′ ) ∈ S ] . \mathbb{P}[M(x)\in S]\leq e^{\varepsilon}\mathbb{P}[M(x^{\prime})\in S]. It can be understood as ensuring a certain level of difficulty in distinguishing whether the output of M M was generated from input x x or input x ′ x^{\prime} , for example, when using a likelihood ratio test as the hypothesis test. Naturally, in all cases, we wish to use the data for some purpose; otherwise, we might as well replace it with pure noise to achieve perfect privacy. Thus, we measure the usefulness of the released data through some utility function u u , and we are interested in maximizing the expected utility 𝔼 ⁡ [ u ⁡ ( M ⁡ ( X ) ) ] \mathbb{E}[u(M(X))] under a given privacy level ϵ \epsilon . Sadly, in virtually all cases of practical interest, maintaining privacy comes at the cost of utility; hence, we seek to characterize the system’s utility-privacy tradeoff ( Chen et al., 2020 ) .

sections.heading: 2.2 Compressing Differential Privacy Mechanisms
sections.text: When the sensitive data is scalar-valued or low-dimensional, it is usually feasible to store or transmit it as-is, uncompressed. However, once the size or dimensionality of the data exceeds a reasonable threshold, such as for image, audio, or video data, compression becomes necessary. The straightforward solution is to apply the mechanism M M first and then losslessly compress the privatized output using, e.g., zip for general data or PNG for images. We consider lossless compression only, as using a lossy compressor could further compromise the utility of the privatized data in ways that are difficult to control. Denoting a lossless compressor as C C , the compressed, privatized code of the data x x is C ⁡ ( M ⁡ ( x ) ) C(M(x)) . A benefit of this solution is that by the post processing property of DP mechanisms ( Dwork & Roth, 2014 ) , if M M is ε \varepsilon -LDP, then so is C ⁡ ( M ⁡ ( x ) ) C(M(x)) . However, in many practical situations, the privatize-then-compress solution quickly reaches a limit: since privacy mechanisms randomize the data, they usually introduce new, albeit random structure. As an extreme example, consider perfectly privatized image compression: we completely uniformly randomize the pixels of the image. In this case, all information is lost, but losslessly compressing each purely random pixel still requires the full bit depth of the image. This is sometimes referred to as the “communication-privacy-accuracy trilemma” ( Chen et al., 2020 ) . This counterintuitive state of affairs is essentially conclusively resolved by the emerging field of stochastic codes ( Flamich & Gündüz, 2026 ) , which we discuss next. Additionally, if the privacy mechanisms rely on continuous noise, such as Gaussian or Laplace noise, it is impossible to compress the privatized data losslessly; see ( Shahmiri et al., 2024 ) for a resolution of this issue for Laplace noise. The inefficiency of the compress-then-privatize approach stems from its sequential structure: the compressor only ever handles the randomized data. In contrast, using stochastic codes allows us to jointly privatize and compress the data, leading to significant improvements in compression rate. Formally, given a conditional distribution P M | X P_{M\mid X} , a stochastic code is a triplet ( Z , enc , dec ) (Z,\enc,\dec) made up of: • A random variable Z Z independent of the input X X , shared between the sender/compressor and the receiver/decompressor, and hence called the common randomness . In practice, Z Z can be realized by using a shared pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) and a common seed for the PRNG. • A function enc ⁡ ( x , z ) \enc(x,z) mapping an input x x and a realization of Z Z to a finite-length bitstring, called the encoder . • A function dec ⁡ ( s , z ) \dec(s,z) mapping a bitstring s s and a realization of Z Z to the support of M M , called the decoder . Finally, to qualify as a stochastic code for P M | X P_{M\mid X} , the triplet must satisfy the requirement that for all x x we have dec ⁡ ( enc ⁡ ( x , Z ) , Z ) ∼ P M | X = x \displaystyle\dec(\enc(x,Z),Z)\sim P_{M\mid X=x} (1) Note that in the above, the randomness arises purely from the synchronized random variable Z Z . Intuitively, one can think of s = enc ⁡ ( x , Z ) s=\enc(x,Z) as encoding a single random sample from P M | X P_{M\mid X} . Somewhat surprisingly, it can be shown that not only can we construct a stochastic code for virtually any conditional distribution P M | X P_{M\mid X} , but we can do so such that the expected codelength 𝔼 ⁡ [ | enc ⁡ ( X , Z ) | ] \mathbb{E}[\lvert\enc(X,Z)\rvert] is close to the mutual information I ⁡ [ M ; X ] I[M\;;\;X] , which is optimal ( Li & El Gamal, 2018 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Flamich, 2024 ) . As we can construct a stochastic code to compress a sample from an arbitrary conditional distribution, and privacy mechanisms may be conceived as conditional distributions, it is a natural next step to combine the two. However, things become more involved regarding the privacy certificate: with stochastic codes, we have the Markov chain X → enc ⁡ ( X , Z ) → dec ⁡ ( enc ⁡ ( X , Z ) , Z ) ⏟ ∼ M ⁡ ( X ) \displaystyle X\to\enc(X,Z)\to\underbrace{\dec(\enc(X,Z),Z)}_{\sim M(X)} (2) as opposed to X → M ⁡ ( X ) → C ⁡ ( M ⁡ ( X ) ) {X\to M(X)\to C(M(X))} as we had with the privatize-then-compress solution. This observation shows that even if M ⁡ ( X ) M(X) is ε \varepsilon -LDP, post processing does not apply and enc ⁡ ( X , Z ) \enc(X,Z) is not immediately ε \varepsilon -LDP. Instead, we need to take special care in constructing ( Z , enc , dec ) (Z,\enc,\dec) so that it can retain (some of) the privacy guarantees of the mechanism M M that it is compressing. The first works to construct such stochastic codes were Feldman & Talwar (2021) ; Triastcyn et al. (2021) and Shah et al. (2022) , however, they have suboptimal compression-privacy performance. Instead, we base our work on the Poisson private representation ( Liu et al., 2024 , PPR;) , the only known stochastic code that exactly simulates arbitrary differential privacy mechanisms with optimal expected codelength.

sections.heading: 2.4 Data Compression with Diffusion Models
sections.text: A diffusion denoising probabilistic model ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 , DDPM;) consists of a fixed forward noising process and a learned reverse denoising process. The forward process gradually corrupts a clean sample x 0 ∼ q ⁡ ( x 0 ) x_{0}\sim q(x_{0}) with Gaussian noise so that, at any time-step t ∈ [ 0 , T ] t\in[0,T] , the marginal admits the closed form x t = γ t ​ x 0 + σ t ​ η t , η t ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) , \displaystyle x_{t}=\gamma_{t}x_{0}+\sigma_{t}\eta_{t},\quad\eta_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathrm{I}), where γ t = 1 − σ t 2 \gamma_{t}=\sqrt{1-\sigma^{2}_{t}} and σ t 2 \sigma^{2}_{t} is a monotonically increasing noise schedule with σ 0 ≈ 0 \sigma_{0}\approx 0 and σ T ≈ 1 \sigma_{T}\approx 1 . We write SNR ⁡ ( t ) = γ t 2 / σ t 2 \mathrm{SNR}(t)=\gamma^{2}_{t}/\sigma^{2}_{t} for the signal-to-noise ratio at time-step t t . The reverse process is parametrized as a Markov chain p θ ​ ( x s ∣ x t ) p_{\theta}(x_{s}\mid x_{t}) trained to minimize the per-step KL divergence D KL [ q ( x s ∣ x t ) ∥ p θ ( x s ∣ x t ) ] {D_{\mathrm{KL}}[q(x_{s}\mid x_{t})\;\|\;p_{\theta}(x_{s}\mid x_{t})]} for s < t {s<t} . Theis et al. (2022) observed that the forward and reverse processes together admit a natural progressive lossy compression interpretation: We can use a stochastic code to encode a sample x s x_{s} from q ⁡ ( x s ∣ x t , x 0 ) q(x_{s}\mid x_{t},x_{0}) using the model proposal p θ ​ ( x s ∣ x t ) p_{\theta}(x_{s}\mid x_{t}) , terminating at any intermediate timestep to trade off bitrate for distortion. Theis et al. (2022) called this framework DiffC and showed that it possesses surprisingly favorable rate-distortion performance, but did not implement it. Indeed, it was first implemented by Vonderfecht & Liu (2025) using latent diffusion models, including Stable Diffusion 1.5/2.1/XL and FLUX.1-dev ( Esser et al., 2024 ) . Although the latter is a rectified flow model, stochastic sampling along its probability flow can be shown to be equivalent to DDPM sampling Lai et al. (2025) , and hence we may use it for DiffC. Flamich & Gündüz (2026) recently revisited the path-based encoding in DiffC from the stochastic coding perspective. They observed that under the assumption of a perfect denoiser, the KL divergence between joint forward and reverse paths on any common discretization s = t 0 < t 1 < ⋯ < t n = T s=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{n}=T equals the KL divergence between their endpoint marginals at s s . This observation means that encoding the final denoising step and the entire denoising path has roughly the same compression cost using stochastic codes. However, encoding the path is now practically feasible. Beyond porting DiffC to large pretrained models, Vonderfecht & Liu (2025) introduced several engineering contributions that bring encoding times down to below 10 seconds. They perform relative entropy coding in fixed-size chunks of approximately 16 bits of KL, splitting high-KL transitions across statistically independent subsets of dimensions, so that each chunk can be feasibly compressed with a stochastic code. Furthermore, they use a custom CUDA kernel for the stochastic code, which draws the candidate samples directly inside the kernel rather than materializing them in GPU memory. Finally, they cast the choice of denoising timestep schedule as a shortest path problem over the cost matrix of pairwise per-step KL divergences. As an ablation, they show that hard-coding the per-encoding-step KL budget across all images, rather than transmitting it as side information, has a negligible effect on the resulting rate-distortion curves.

sections.heading: 3 Approximate PPR
sections.text: As we mentioned in Section 2.2 , PPR encodes an arbitrary LDP mechanism P M | X P_{M\mid X} using a coding distribution Q M Q_{M} with as short a codelength as possible. However, PPR’s exactness can be a drawback: its runtime scales as ‖ d ​ P M | X d ​ Q M ‖ ∞ \left\lVert\frac{dP_{M\mid X}}{dQ_{M}}\right\rVert_{\infty} , which can be infinite even when D KL [ P M | X ∥ Q M ] D_{\mathrm{KL}}[P_{M\mid X}\;\|\;Q_{M}] is finite. We address this issue by developing an approximate variant of PPR whose output is no longer an exact sample from P M | X P_{M\mid X} but is still suitably close, as measured by the total variation distance. Furthermore, this variant will retain its close-to-optimal expected codelength and its average runtime scales as 𝒪 ( exp ( D KL [ P M | X ∥ Q M ] ) ) \mathcal{O}(\exp(D_{\mathrm{KL}}[P_{M\mid X}\;\|\;Q_{M}])) . sections.heading: 4.1 The Denoising Process as a Privacy Mechanism
sections.text: Our most important high-level observation is that, the DDPM denoising process conditioned on the original image x 0 x_{0} is a valid privacy mechanism . Concretely, at each denoising timestep, we may view a sample from the conditional posterior given in Equation 6 as an additive Gaussian privacy mechanism for x 0 x_{0} : M ⁡ ( x 0 ) = μ q ​ ( x t , x 0 , s , t ) + σ ⁡ ( s , t ) ​ η , η ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \displaystyle M(x_{0})\!=\!\mu_{q}(x_{t},x_{0};s,t)+\sigma(s,t)\,\eta,\quad\eta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathrm{I}) (17) We defer the discussion on the privacy guarantee of this mechanism to Appendix A . Unfortunately, the Gaussian mechanism does not yield a pure ϵ \epsilon -LDP certificate, and hence our Theorem 3.1 does not apply if we apply step-limited PPR to it. To circumvent this issue, we moment-match Laplace distributions to the Gaussian targets and proposals at each time step and use those for denoising and compression instead. sections.heading: 4.2 Compressing the Privacy Mechanism
sections.text: In DiffC ( Theis et al., 2022 ) , the output of each denoising step is not released directly, but compressed via a stochastic code; in our case, this is where we will apply the PPR code. Under PPR, at each step we compress the privacy mechanism M t → s ​ ( x 0 ) M_{t\rightarrow s}(x_{0}) and the compressed output inherits a privacy guarantee that depends on PPR’s parameter α \alpha and the privacy parameters of the mechanism being compressed. Note that in the works of Theis et al. (2022) and Vonderfecht & Liu (2025) , the code they used is equivalent to our PPR code with the parameter α = ∞ \alpha=\infty , which achieves maximal compression efficiency but provides no privacy guarantee. However, as we explained in Section 2.3 , exact PPR (that is, the budget is n = ∞ n=\infty ) requires an upper bound on the density ratio between the target and the proposal distributions. In the Gaussian case of Equation 17 , both distributions are Gaussians with the same variance q = 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ q , σ 2 ​ I ) , p = 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ p , σ 2 ​ I ) , \displaystyle q=\mathcal{N}(\mu_{q},\sigma^{2}\mathrm{I}),\,p=\mathcal{N}(\mu_{p},\sigma^{2}\mathrm{I}), (20) whose density ratio is easily seen to be unbounded. Fortunately, with our moment-matched Laplace distributions ( Equation 18 ) this is no longer an issue: the density ratio of two Laplace distributions with the same scale is always bounded. However, despite the density ratio no longer being an issue, step-limited PPR still provides a significant computational advantage compared to its exact variant. Since we choose the step-budget n n ahead of time, we can draw the n n proposal samples and evaluate their density ratios in parallel on a GPU using a custom CUDA kernel (see Appendix B ). Thus, we use step-limited PPR ( Definition 2 ). Combining it with the per-step, per-pixel guarantee derived in Section 4.1 , the PPR code satisfies a 2 ​ α ​ ϵ t → s 2\alpha\epsilon_{t\rightarrow s} -LDP per-pixel guarantee at each step. By sequential composition, the total per-pixel privacy certificate across n n encoding steps is: ϵ total = 2 ​ α ​ ∑ i = 1 n ϵ t i → t i − 1 \displaystyle\epsilon_{\text{total}}=2\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{t_{i}\rightarrow t_{i-1}} We show experimentally that, for compression to the same final timestep, replacing the Gaussian channel with the moment-matched Laplace channel and α = ∞ \alpha=\infty with α = 2 \alpha=2 in step-limited PPR has a negligible effect on the downstream task, while increasing the bitrate by a factor of ≈ 2 \approx 2 ; see the bottom left panel of Figure 1 . The factor 2 2 increase can be in large part explained by comparing the relative entropies between the original Gaussians involved and their moment-matched Laplace counterparts, see Appendix C .

sections.heading: 5.2 Classification
sections.text: The pretrained DDPM model ( Ho et al., 2020 ) used as the backbone of our compression schemes has been trained on the CIFAR-10 training set. Hence, to prevent data leakage, we use the CIFAR-10 test set, split evenly into 5k training and 5k evaluation images to train and evaluate our classifier. To measure how privacy affects downstream utility, we follow the protocol of Cao et al. (2026) and train a ResNet-56 classifier directly on the privatized images. The classifier never sees clean data; it is trained in the noisy domain using the provided image labels, using the same hyperparameters as Cao et al. (2026) to enable direct comparison.

sections.heading: 5.3 The DiffC Baseline
sections.text: We compare DP-DiPP to the original Gaussian DiffC ( Vonderfecht & Liu, 2025 ) , which is equivalent to our step-limited PPR algorithm with α = ∞ \alpha=\infty . Note that Gaussian noise lacks a pure LDP guarantee, and so does using PPR with α = ∞ \alpha=\infty ; we include it as an ablation to show that DP-DiPP’s performance does not degrade significantly when using moment-matched Laplace distributions instead of the original Gaussians. To ensure a fair comparison between DiffC and DP-DiPP, we first solve the resource-constrained shortest path problem for the DP-DiPP mechanism at each privacy level ϵ \epsilon . After we decide on a final timestep T final T_{\text{final}} , we find the shortest path for DiffC that leads to T final T_{\text{final}} .

sections.heading: 5.4 Empirical Findings
sections.text: Our experimental results are shown in Figure 1 . Each point on the curve represents a final compression timestep, after which each method uses the DDPM denoiser to complete denoising the images. For our experiments, we tuned each method to attain a per-pixel ϵ \epsilon -LDP certificate (or equivalent in the case of DiffC) for ϵ ∈ { 1 , 4 , 16 , 64 , 256 } \epsilon\in\{1,4,16,64,256\} . For the step-limited PPR code in DP-DiPP, we set α = 2 \alpha=2 . First and foremost, our findings validate our method: DP-DiPP’s joint privatization and compression significantly outperform the privatize-then-compress baseline, as shown in the top row of Figure 1 . In particular, DP-DiPP achieves the same classification accuracy (top left panel) and the same LDP guarantee (top right panel) using less than 3-11% of the bits that the baseline method needs, yielding a 10-30 × \times improvement in the rate! Second, in the bottom row of Figure 1 , comparison of DiffC and DP-DiPP shows that using moment-matched Laplace distributions instead of Gaussians and a strict privacy parameter of α = 2 \alpha=2 introduces a roughly 2-times penalty in the rate (bottom right), while the utility is largely unaffected.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion and Future Directions
sections.text: We introduced an approximate version of PPR and showed that it retains an LDP guarantee and has good approximation properties. Then, we applied it to diffusion-based compression, and showed that using Laplace instead of Gaussian denoising distributions can significantly improve the formal privacy guarantee while retaining empirical performance. We applied our method to image compression on CIFAR-10 and showed that our joint compression method significantly outperforms the privatize-then-compress baseline. We have only dealt with pure ϵ \epsilon -LDP mechanisms. Thus, a future theoretical direction could be to consider whether it is possible to construct approximate versions of PPR from mechanisms that are ( ϵ , δ ) (\epsilon,\delta) -LDP instead.

Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled framework with strong formal guarantees and has already achieved practical success. However, releasing high-dimensional data, such as images, has remained elusive: releasing uncompressed privatized data requires significant storage. At the same time, no effective data compression scheme exists that can compress high-resolution data with privacy guarantees. We address this challenge with DP-DiPP , a compression pipeline that combines stochastic codes with diffusion models. DP-DiPP is highly flexible: the practitioner has direct control over the compression rate-privacy-utility tradeoff. As the theoretical backbone, we extend the Poisson private representation (PPR) of ( Liu et al., 2024 ) to encode the outputs of privacy mechanisms. We then combine it with DiffC, a diffusion-based lossy data compression method, to obtain a differentially private image compressor. Our experiments on privatized image classification on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that DP-DiPP significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving a 10-30 times better compression while retaining comparable privacy guarantees and utility. Keywords: diffusion model, stochastic code, data compression, differential privacy, relative entropy coding 1 Introduction Over the past decades, the rapid growth in data collection and its use in downstream systems such as machine learning has produced undeniable benefits. Yet, this has also raised serious concerns about the identifiability of sensitive information and individual privacy. Therefore, developing frameworks and algorithms that protect privacy is essential to ensure user trust. In this paper, we adopt differential privacy (DP) as the privacy framework, a stronger variant of DP ( Dwork et al., 2006 ; Dwork & Roth, 2014 , DP;) . DP has already found practical success, such as for collecting user data ( Erlingsson et al., 2014 ) , for releasing privatized tabular data, like census data ( United States Census Bureau, 2021 ) , and for preventing generative models from memorizing and revealing their training sets ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . Local DP (LDP) protects individuals’ data by requiring that a system’s output reveal only limited information about its input. In practice, this idea translates to randomizing the sensitive data X X before revealing it to an untrusted party, according to a privacy mechanism . For example, if X X represents location data, such as GPS coordinates ( Andrés et al., 2013 ) , one possible privacy mechanism is to add appropriately calibrated noise η \eta to the coordinates to prevent precise localization, that is, Y = X + η Y=X+\eta . Of course, we still wish to use the privatized data for some purpose. Hence, a natural tradeoff arises between the privatized data’s utility for its downstream task and its privacy guarantee. However, despite its success for tabular data, scaling DP to high-dimensional data such as images, audio, or video remains challenging. This difficulty stems from several factors. First, directly releasing privatized high-dimensional data can incur substantial storage and communication costs. Second, the noise required to provide meaningful privacy guarantees can severely degrade the data’s utility in high-dimensional domains. To the best of our knowledge, prior work has not systematically studied high-resolution privatized data compression, where the goal is to jointly preserve privacy, reduce storage cost, and retain downstream utility. This is the challenge we tackle in this paper. The theoretical foundation of our work is in the emerging field of data compression with stochastic codes ( Flamich, 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Flamich & Gündüz, 2026 ) . In practice, stochastic codes serve as a randomized lossy compression mechanism : for example, consider an input X X (modeled as a random variable) and a perturbed, lossy version Y = X + η Y=X+\eta , where η \eta is independent of X X . Then, for a given X X , stochastic codes produce a bitstring S S that encodes one sample of Y | X Y\mid X , such that the expected length of S S is as small as possible. By utilizing stochastic codes, the generated sample exactly follows the conditional distribution. This is in sharp contrast to traditional lossy compression, where we first construct a quantizer and then attempt to determine the quantizer’s error distribution. This flexibility of stochastic codes naturally suggests their application to compressing the output of privacy mechanisms, where the exactness of sample distribution preserves other desirable statistical properties of the original privacy mechanism, such as unbiasedness and Gaussianity. Unfortunately, as we explain in Section 2.2 , simply encoding the outputs of privacy mechanisms with stochastic codes can lose the privacy guarantees of the original mechanism; hence, we need to design special-purpose codes that preserve the guarantees. As a solution, we use the Poisson private representation ( Liu et al., 2024 , PPR;) as a starting point for our work, a stochastic code that does have LDP guarantees. Concretely, we develop an approximate version (called “step-limited” in this paper) of PPR that encodes any pure ϵ \epsilon -LDP mechanism, ensuring that its output is at least 2 ​ α ​ ϵ 2\alpha\epsilon -LDP, where α > 1 \alpha>1 is a tunable parameter that interpolates between the code’s privacy and the expected codelength. Unfortunately, applying PPR to complex data is challenging due to its generally very slow runtime, scaling super-exponentially with the information content. To circumvent this issue, we combine our extended PPR code with DiffC, a variable-rate, diffusion-based data compression framework ( Theis et al., 2022 ) . DiffC progressively encodes each denoising step of a Gaussian diffusion model, thereby decomposing the compression problem into smaller, manageable steps. However, additive Gaussian noise never yields a pure ϵ \epsilon -LDP mechanism. Hence, we approximate the Gaussian denoising targets at each step with moment-matched Laplace distributions, which do provide pure ϵ \epsilon -LDP guarantees, allowing us to apply our approximate PPR code. Somewhat surprisingly, we empirically find that this approximation does not degrade the denoiser’s performance, while significantly strengthening its formal privacy guarantee. Thus, we call our method Differentially Private DiffC with Poisson Processes (DP-DiPP, pronounced dippy-dip ). Put succinctly, DP-DiPP jointly compresses and privatizes the data, rather than privatizing the data first and then compressing it losslessly. Thus, to validate our method, we conduct experiments on privatized image compression and classification on CIFAR-10 and compare it with the naive method. We find that DP-DiPP performs significantly better, consistently reducing bitrate by a factor of 10-30 while maintaining a comparable pure LDP guarantee and utility (as measured by classification accuracy). In summary, our main contributions are as follows: • In Section 3 , we extend the Poisson private representation (PPR) of Liu et al. (2024) to approximate sampling, and analyze its output sample quality and its DP guarantees. Notably, we show that it yields a 2 ​ α ​ ϵ 2\alpha\epsilon -LDP certificate when used to encode any pure ϵ \epsilon -LDP mechanism, where α ≥ 1 \alpha\geq 1 is a tunable parameter that trades off privacy and approximation quality. • In Section 4 , we modify DiffC, a variable-rate, Gaussian diffusion-based lossy data compression method, by replacing the Gaussian targets in the denoising process with Laplace distributions, which turns the reverse process into a pure ϵ \epsilon -LDP mechanism. Surprisingly, we show that this approximation does not significantly degrade the denoiser’s performance. • In Section 5 , we apply our approximate PPR code to the modified DiffC process, yielding our proposed method, DP-DiPP , and validate its performance on a privatized image compression task on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Our results show that DP-DiPP consistently reduces bitrate by a factor of 10-30 while maintaining a comparable pure LDP guarantee and utility (as measured by classification accuracy). 1.1 Notation We denote the binary logarithm as log \log . In this paper, we concern ourselves with its strict variant, local DP (LDP): we take some sensitive input x x and randomize it using a privacy mechanism M ⁡ ( x ) M(x) to reduce the information leaked by x x . However, not any randomization will do: in ε \varepsilon -LDP we choose a privacy parameter ε ≥ 0 \varepsilon\geq 0 and require the mechanism M M to satisfy, for any two inputs x , x ′ x,x^{\prime} and any measurable event S S , ℙ [ M ( x ) ∈ S ] ≤ e ε ℙ [ M ( x ′ ) ∈ S ] . \mathbb{P}[M(x)\in S]\leq e^{\varepsilon}\mathbb{P}[M(x^{\prime})\in S]. It can be understood as ensuring a certain level of difficulty in distinguishing whether the output of M M was generated from input x x or input x ′ x^{\prime} , for example, when using a likelihood ratio test as the hypothesis test. Naturally, in all cases, we wish to use the data for some purpose; otherwise, we might as well replace it with pure noise to achieve perfect privacy. Thus, we measure the usefulness of the released data through some utility function u u , and we are interested in maximizing the expected utility 𝔼 ⁡ [ u ⁡ ( M ⁡ ( X ) ) ] \mathbb{E}[u(M(X))] under a given privacy level ϵ \epsilon . Sadly, in virtually all cases of practical interest, maintaining privacy comes at the cost of utility; hence, we seek to characterize the system’s utility-privacy tradeoff ( Chen et al., 2020 ) . 2.2 Compressing Differential Privacy Mechanisms When the sensitive data is scalar-valued or low-dimensional, it is usually feasible to store or transmit it as-is, uncompressed. However, once the size or dimensionality of the data exceeds a reasonable threshold, such as for image, audio, or video data, compression becomes necessary. The straightforward solution is to apply the mechanism M M first and then losslessly compress the privatized output using, e.g., zip for general data or PNG for images. We consider lossless compression only, as using a lossy compressor could further compromise the utility of the privatized data in ways that are difficult to control. Denoting a lossless compressor as C C , the compressed, privatized code of the data x x is C ⁡ ( M ⁡ ( x ) ) C(M(x)) . A benefit of this solution is that by the post processing property of DP mechanisms ( Dwork & Roth, 2014 ) , if M M is ε \varepsilon -LDP, then so is C ⁡ ( M ⁡ ( x ) ) C(M(x)) . However, in many practical situations, the privatize-then-compress solution quickly reaches a limit: since privacy mechanisms randomize the data, they usually introduce new, albeit random structure. As an extreme example, consider perfectly privatized image compression: we completely uniformly randomize the pixels of the image. In this case, all information is lost, but losslessly compressing each purely random pixel still requires the full bit depth of the image. This is sometimes referred to as the “communication-privacy-accuracy trilemma” ( Chen et al., 2020 ) . This counterintuitive state of affairs is essentially conclusively resolved by the emerging field of stochastic codes ( Flamich & Gündüz, 2026 ) , which we discuss next. Additionally, if the privacy mechanisms rely on continuous noise, such as Gaussian or Laplace noise, it is impossible to compress the privatized data losslessly; see ( Shahmiri et al., 2024 ) for a resolution of this issue for Laplace noise. The inefficiency of the compress-then-privatize approach stems from its sequential structure: the compressor only ever handles the randomized data. In contrast, using stochastic codes allows us to jointly privatize and compress the data, leading to significant improvements in compression rate. Formally, given a conditional distribution P M | X P_{M\mid X} , a stochastic code is a triplet ( Z , enc , dec ) (Z,\enc,\dec) made up of: • A random variable Z Z independent of the input X X , shared between the sender/compressor and the receiver/decompressor, and hence called the common randomness . The first works to construct such stochastic codes were Feldman & Talwar (2021) ; Triastcyn et al. (2021) and Shah et al. (2022) , however, they have suboptimal compression-privacy performance.
